questions.q: Riya lists the things she saw on a forest visit with her teacher. Which pair from her list are BOTH abiotic components of the forest habitat?
questions.a: Soil and temperature

questions.q: According to the chapter, which of these best describes a habitat?
questions.a: The place where an organism lives
o: The place where an organism lives
Only a large forest where wild animals live
The food that an organism eats each day
A group of organisms of the same kind

questions.q: In one forest, an owl hunts at night and a squirrel is active during the day. Which statement about the two animals fits the chapter?
questions.a: They share one habitat but face different conditions, such as temperature
o: They share one habitat but face different conditions, such as temperature
They live in two different habitats because they are active at different times
They face exactly the same conditions because they share one habitat
Only the squirrel uses abiotic components, since sunlight is absent at night

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In states such as Odisha and Assam, elephants sometimes damage banana and sugarcane crops in farms.
Reason (R): Wildlife corridors connect forest habitats so that elephants can travel between large forest areas.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Define the biotic and the abiotic components of a habitat. Give one example of each from a forest habitat.
questions.a: Biotic components are the living beings of a habitat (plants, animals and microbes); abiotic components are its non-living things (air, water, soil, sunlight and temperature). Forest example: biotic - grass, trees or birds; abiotic - soil, sunlight or air.
s: Both terms defined: biotic = the living beings, abiotic = the non-living things of a habitat
One correct forest example of each, such as trees (biotic) and soil (abiotic)

questions.q:
(a) Name two changes, given in the chapter, that make forests dry up and shrink.
(b) Why do elephants then enter farms and villages?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: changes in rainfall, changes in temperature, cutting down trees to build roads and buildings. (b) When vegetation becomes scarce and waterholes dry up, their forest habitat no longer meets their needs, so they wander into farms in search of food such as bananas and sugarcane.
s: (a) Two correct changes, such as changes in rainfall and cutting trees for roads and buildings
(b) Loss of habitat: scarce vegetation and dry waterholes push elephants into farms in search of food

questions.q:
Answer briefly about fish in a pond.
(a) Name any two conditions a pond provides that are essential for the survival of its organisms.
(b) Name one biotic need of a fish and say where it comes from.
(c) Name one abiotic need of a fish and say where it comes from.
questions.a: (a) Any two of food, oxygen, shelter and space to grow. (b) Food, which comes from small plants and animals in the pond. (c) Oxygen, which comes from the water.
s: (a) Two of food, oxygen, shelter and space to grow
(b) Food, from small plants and animals
(c) Oxygen, from the water

questions.q: Kabir says: 'A pond and a forest both have living beings and non-living things, so the same kinds of organisms can live in both.' Is Kabir right, wrong or partly right? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. He is right that both habitats have biotic and abiotic components. He is wrong about the organisms: the kinds of living beings differ, and the non-living conditions (air, sunlight, water, temperature and soil) vary from habitat to habitat. Every organism needs specific conditions to survive, so a fish, which takes its oxygen from water, lives in the pond and not on the forest floor.
s: Verdict: partly right
Correct part named: both habitats have biotic and abiotic components
Wrong part explained: conditions differ and each organism needs specific conditions, with an example such as a fish needing water

questions.q:
A village in Assam lies beside a forest. The panchayat kept this record (illustrative figures). In 2015 the forest beside the village covered 50 sq km, and elephants entered the village fields 6 times in the year. By 2023 a road and new buildings had been built and there had been two dry years; the forest covered 35 sq km, and elephants entered the fields 21 times, mostly raiding banana plantations.
(a) What is a habitat, and what is the natural habitat of these elephants?
(b) By what percentage did the forest shrink from 2015 to 2023, and how many times as many field visits were there in 2023 as in 2015?
(c) Using the chapter, explain why the visits rose as the forest shrank.
(d) The panchayat can afford only one plan: (i) digging a trench around the banana fields, or (ii) working with forest officers to keep a marked corridor to the next large forest free of buildings. Which plan deals with the cause the chapter describes? Give one limit of that plan.
questions.a: (a) A habitat is the place where an organism lives and finds the conditions it needs; these elephants' natural habitat is the forest. (b) Shrink = (50 - 35) / 50 x 100 = 30%; visits = 21 / 6 = 3.5 times as many. (c) Cutting trees for the road and buildings, and the dry years, shrank and dried the forest, so vegetation became scarce and waterholes dried up; having lost habitat, the elephants moved into the fields in search of food such as bananas. (d) The corridor plan: a corridor lets elephants travel between large forest areas without coming into the village, so it deals with the loss of habitat. Its limit: it does not bring back the 15 sq km of forest already lost, so the remaining forest must also be protected.
s: (a) Habitat defined as the place where an organism lives; the elephants' habitat is the forest
(b) 30% shrink and 3.5 times as many visits
(c) A smaller, drier forest means scarce food and water, so elephants enter fields in search of food
(d) Corridor plan chosen with its reason (safe movement between forests) and one limit stated

questions.q:
With their teacher, students observe a large banyan tree in their school. They note: squirrels, ants, myna birds, a snake that lives in a hollow of the trunk and comes out at night, the soil around the roots, sunlight, air and rainwater on the leaves.
(a) Can a single tree be a habitat? Give a reason.
(b) List the biotic components they noted.
(c) List the abiotic components they noted.
(d) The snake comes out at night and the squirrels are active by day. Do they face the same conditions?
(e) Name one need the squirrel meets from the biotic part of this habitat and one it meets from the abiotic part.
questions.a: (a) Yes; a habitat is simply the place where an organism lives, and it can even be just the bark of a tree, so a large banyan tree is a habitat. (b) Biotic: squirrels, ants, myna birds, the snake (and the banyan tree itself). (c) Abiotic: soil, sunlight, air and rainwater. (d) No; they share the habitat, but the day is warmer than the night, so they face different conditions; this is how they live together in the same habitat. (e) Biotic: food, such as the tree's fruits; abiotic: oxygen from the air (or water).
s: (a) Yes, with the reason that a habitat is where an organism lives and can be as small as a tree
(b) Correct list of the living components
(c) Correct list of the non-living components
(d) No: warm day and cool night mean different conditions in the same habitat
(e) One biotic need (food) and one abiotic need (oxygen or water)

questions.q: Which of these is a population?
questions.a: All the lotus plants of one kind in a pond
o: All the lotus plants of one kind in a pond
All the plants and animals living in a pond
The water, soil and lotus plants of a pond
A single lotus plant growing in a pond

questions.q: Researchers record four ponds, each with the same kinds of flowering plants around it. Going by the chapter's pond study, near which pond would the flowers be expected to produce the most seeds?
questions.a: A pond with fish, few dragonflies and many bees
o: A pond with fish, few dragonflies and many bees
A pond without fish, many dragonflies and few bees
A pond without fish, many dragonflies and few flies
A pond with fish, many dragonflies and few butterflies

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
Column I: 1. Population, 2. Community, 3. Pollination, 4. Stamen
Column II: A. Male part of a flower that releases pollen, B. Different populations sharing the same habitat, C. Organisms of the same type in a habitat at a given time, D. Carrying pollen from stamens to carpels
What is a community? Name any three members of the community of a pond.
questions.a: A community is made up of the different populations that share the same habitat; its plants, animals and microorganisms interact and depend on one another. Pond members: any three of fish, frogs, turtles, snails, ducks, dragonflies, algae, duckweed and lotus.
s: Community defined as the different populations sharing one habitat
Three correct members of a pond community

questions.q: True or False? 'In the chapter's pond study, fish helped the plants near the pond to produce more seeds, even though the fish ate neither the flowers nor the bees.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Fish eat dragonfly larvae, so ponds with fish have fewer dragonflies. Dragonflies eat bees, flies and butterflies, so with fewer dragonflies more of these pollinators survive, more flowers are pollinated and more seeds form. The effect of the fish on the seeds is indirect.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: fish eat dragonfly larvae, fewer dragonflies leave more pollinators, so more flowers are pollinated and more seeds form

questions.q:
In a 1 m x 1 m patch of a school garden, students count 18 plants of one kind of grass and 6 plants of one kind of daisy on the same morning.
(a) How many plant populations did they count?
(b) How many times as large as the daisy population is the grass population?
questions.a: (a) 2 populations, one of the grass and one of the daisy. (b) 18 / 6 = 3 times as large.
s: (a) 2 populations
(b) 18 / 6 = 3 times

questions.q:
(a) Name the female and the male reproductive parts of a flower.
(b) Name any two agents that carry pollen between flowers.
(c) Why is pollination important for a plant?
questions.a: (a) Female: carpels; male: stamens. (b) Any two of wind, water, insects, bats and birds. (c) Pollination is essential for the formation of fruits and seeds.
s: (a) Carpels (female) and stamens (male)
(b) Two of wind, water, insects, bats and birds
(c) It is essential for forming fruits and seeds

questions.q: Neel visits a pond without fish and sees many dragonflies darting over the flowers. He concludes: 'Dragonflies must help these flowers make more seeds, because they fly from flower to flower.' Use the chapter's pond study to test his conclusion.
questions.a: His conclusion is wrong. Dragonflies eat bees, flies and butterflies, which are the insects that pollinate the flowers. Many dragonflies mean fewer pollinators, so fewer flowers are pollinated and fewer seeds form; that is why flowers near ponds without fish may produce fewer seeds than those near ponds with fish.
s: Verdict: the conclusion is wrong
Dragonflies eat bees, flies and butterflies, the pollinators
More dragonflies lead to fewer pollinators, less pollination and fewer seeds

questions.a: (a) Fish eat dragonfly larvae, so the number of dragonflies will fall. (b) Dragonflies eat bees, flies and butterflies, so with fewer dragonflies more of these insects will survive. (c) More pollinators will carry pollen between the mustard flowers, so more flowers are pollinated and more seeds may form. (d) He can welcome the plan, since the fish indirectly help pollination; but if the pond were later overfished, the dragonflies would increase again, the pollinators would fall and his seed yield could drop, so the fish should not be overfished.
s: (a) Fish eat dragonfly larvae, so dragonflies decrease
(b) Fewer dragonflies, so more bees, flies and butterflies survive
(c) More pollination, so more mustard seeds
(d) Welcomes the plan with the reason, and explains that overfishing would reverse the chain and lower the yield

questions.q:
The eco-club of a school in Guwahati marked a 1 m x 1 m square in the school garden. At 8 a.m. on one day they counted: Plant X, 28; Plant Y, 7; ants, 40; earthworms, 3. After rain, when they counted again at 8 p.m. on the same day, they found 11 earthworms on the surface.
(a) How many populations did they count in the morning?
(b) Do all the organisms in the square together form a population or a community? Why?
(c) How many times as large as the population of Plant Y is the population of Plant X?
(d) A member says the morning earthworm count was wrong because the evening count was different. Is she right? Use the meaning of population.
questions.a: (a) 4 populations: Plant X, Plant Y, ants and earthworms. (b) A community, because they are different populations sharing the same habitat. (c) 28 / 7 = 4 times as large. (d) No; a population is the group of one type of organism in a habitat at a given time, so 3 earthworms at 8 a.m. and 11 at 8 p.m. can both be correct for their own times.
s: (a) 4 populations
(b) A community, since they are different populations in one habitat
(c) 28 / 7 = 4 times
(d) No: a population is counted at a given time, so both counts can be correct

questions.q: 'Water in a pond is evaporating fast because of the bright sunlight.' Which kind of interaction does this observation show?
questions.a: Between two abiotic components
o: Between a biotic and an abiotic component
Between a producer and a consumer

questions.q: Which order runs correctly from the smallest level of organisation to the largest?
questions.a: Individual, population, community, ecosystem

questions.q:
Read these statements about ecosystems.
I. Ponds, rivers and lakes are aquatic ecosystems.
II. A farmland is a terrestrial ecosystem that formed without any human role.
III. Plant roots holding soil in place is an example of a biotic component influencing an abiotic one.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The abiotic components of an ecosystem can be changed by its biotic components.
Reason (R): Plants release oxygen during photosynthesis, and their roots hold soil in place and prevent erosion.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: What is an ecosystem? Name its two main types, with one example of each.
questions.a: An ecosystem is formed when the biotic components (plants, animals and microorganisms) and the abiotic components (air, water, soil, sunlight and temperature) of a habitat interact with each other. Types: aquatic, such as a pond, river or lake; terrestrial, such as a forest, a farm or a large tree.
s: Ecosystem defined as the biotic and abiotic components of a habitat interacting with each other
Aquatic and terrestrial named, with one correct example of each

questions.q: True or False? 'Living things depend on air, water, soil and sunlight, but these non-living things are never changed by living things.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. Abiotic components are also influenced by biotic components: plants release oxygen during photosynthesis, their roots hold soil in place and prevent erosion, and plants retain soil moisture and help cool the atmosphere.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: one way living things change abiotic components, such as plants releasing oxygen or roots holding soil

questions.q:
State which kind of interaction each observation shows: between a biotic and an abiotic component, between two abiotic components, or among biotic components.
(a) A lotus plant takes root in the mud at the bottom of a pond.
(b) The midday sun warms the water at the surface of a pond.
(c) A heron catches and eats a frog.
questions.a: (a) Between a biotic and an abiotic component (the lotus and the mud). (b) Between two abiotic components (sunlight and water). (c) Among biotic components (the heron and the frog).
s: (a) Biotic and abiotic
(b) Two abiotic components
(c) Among biotic components

questions.q:
For a school garden, write one observation of your own for each kind of interaction below, and say what it influences, as the chapter describes.
(a) Between a biotic and an abiotic component
(b) Between two abiotic components
(c) Among biotic components
questions.a: Sample answer. (a) Marigold roots take up water from the soil; this influences a life process (nutrition) of the plant. (b) Strong sunlight dries the wet soil of a flower bed; this influences the physical characteristics of the habitat. (c) A myna eats earthworms from the lawn; this influences the availability of resources (food) needed for life processes. Any correct observation of each kind, with what it influences, earns the mark.
s: (a) A correct biotic-abiotic observation, influencing a life process such as nutrition, respiration or reproduction
(b) A correct abiotic-abiotic observation, influencing the physical characteristics of the habitat
(c) A correct biotic-biotic observation, influencing the availability of resources such as food

questions.q:
A school in Jaipur has a small pond on its campus. In May, students and their teacher recorded (illustrative figures): the water was 24 degrees C at 7 a.m. and 36 degrees C at 2 p.m.; with no rain, the water depth fell from 80 cm on 1 May to 62 cm on 31 May; and the shallow, plant-filled edge where fish laid their eggs dried out. The school now plans to plant shady trees on the banks of the pond.
(a) Which kind of interaction is 'the water level falls because sunlight makes the water evaporate'?
(b) By how many centimetres, and by what percentage, did the depth fall in May?
(c) Explain how the drying edge affects a biotic component of the pond.
(d) Is planting trees on the banks a sensible step? Use the chapter's ideas about how biotic components influence abiotic ones, and name one thing the trees cannot fix.
questions.a: (a) An interaction between two abiotic components (sunlight and water). (b) 80 - 62 = 18 cm; 18 / 80 x 100 = 22.5%. (c) Fish lay their eggs in water near vegetation to protect them from other fish or frogs; with the plant-filled edge dry, they lose these safe places, so their reproduction is affected. (d) Yes, it is sensible: plants retain soil moisture and help cool the surroundings, and their roots hold the soil of the banks in place, so the trees can reduce heating and drying. But trees do not add water; the pond still depends on rain to refill it, so the step helps but does not solve the problem alone.
s: (a) Two abiotic components
(b) 18 cm and 22.5%
(c) Loss of the plant-filled edge where fish lay eggs affects fish reproduction
(d) Judgement that trees help (moisture, cooling, roots hold soil) with the limit that they cannot add water

questions.a: (a) The community is all the populations living in the lake, such as fish, frogs, snails, algae and lotus. (b) Any two of water, soil, air, sunlight and temperature. (c) For example, fish take oxygen from the water, or water plants use sunlight, carbon dioxide and water to make food. (d) For example, water plants release oxygen into the water during photosynthesis, or plant roots hold the soil of the banks in place. (e) One fish is an individual; all the fish of its kind form a population; all the populations together form the community; and the community interacting with the water, soil, air and sunlight forms the ecosystem. So the ecosystem holds the community plus its abiotic components and their interactions.
s: (a) Community as all the populations in the lake, with two members
(b) Two abiotic components
(c) One correct dependence of organisms on abiotic components
(d) One correct way organisms change abiotic components
(e) Individual to population to community to ecosystem, with the ecosystem including the abiotic part

questions.q: Why are green plants called autotrophs?
questions.a: They make their own food
o: They eat other organisms for food
They break down dead plants and animals

questions.q: In a crop field, millet is eaten by mice, mice are eaten by snakes, and snakes are eaten by eagles. Eagles also catch mice directly. Counting the producer as the first trophic level, at which trophic level or levels does the eagle appear in this field's food chains?
questions.a: Third and fourth

questions.q:
Match each organism in Column I with its group in Column II.
Column I: 1. Deer, 2. Leopard, 3. Fox, 4. Mushroom
Column II: A. Decomposer, B. Herbivore, C. Carnivore, D. Omnivore

Assertion (A): A food web is a single straight line that shows who eats whom in an ecosystem.
Reason (R): In an ecosystem, each organism may be eaten by two or more types of organisms.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q:
Look at this food chain: grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake -> eagle.
(a) Name the producer in it.
(b) At which trophic level is the frog?
questions.a: (a) Grass. (b) The third trophic level: grass is first, the grasshopper second and the frog third.
s: (a) Grass is the producer
(b) The frog is at the third trophic level

questions.q: True or False? 'A mouse is a heterotroph, even though much of its food is plant seeds.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. A mouse cannot make its own food and depends on other organisms for it, so it is a heterotroph (a consumer). Eating plants does not make it an autotroph; the chapter in fact lists mice as omnivores, eating both plants and animals.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: it cannot make its own food and depends on other organisms, so it is a heterotroph

questions.q:
In a grassland, grasshoppers and mice eat grass; frogs eat grasshoppers; snakes eat frogs and mice; hawks eat snakes and mice.
(a) Write the longest food chain in this grassland.
(b) Write the shortest food chain that ends with the hawk.
(c) Why do these chains together form a food web?
questions.a: (a) Grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake -> hawk. (b) Grass -> mouse -> hawk. (c) Some organisms are eaten by more than one type of organism (the mouse is eaten by both snakes and hawks, and the snake is fed by both frogs and mice), so the food chains are interlinked into a network, which is a food web.
s: (a) Grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake -> hawk
(b) Grass -> mouse -> hawk
(c) Organisms eaten by more than one type link the chains into a network, the food web

questions.q: Rina says: 'A frog and a tiger are both carnivores, so they must be at the same trophic level.' Is she right, wrong or partly right? Explain using the chapter's trophic levels.
questions.a: Partly right. Both are carnivores, since both eat animals. But a trophic level is an organism's position in a food chain: small carnivores such as frogs are at the third trophic level, while large carnivores such as tigers occupy the next level. So they are not at the same trophic level.
s: Verdict: partly right
Correct part: both are carnivores because they eat animals
Wrong part: frogs (small carnivores) are at the third level and tigers (large carnivores) at the next level

questions.q:
Farmers beside a grassland in Maharashtra kept a yearly count on a 1-hectare plot (illustrative figures). The feeding links there are grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake -> eagle. In Year 1 they counted 400 grasshoppers, 60 frogs, 8 snakes and 2 eagles. During Year 2 people killed most of the snakes out of fear. In Year 3 they counted 250 grasshoppers, 105 frogs, 1 snake and no eagle on the plot.
(a) Name the producer, and give the trophic level of the snake.
(b) By what percentage did the frogs rise, and the grasshoppers fall, from Year 1 to Year 3?
(c) Explain the change in the frogs and the grasshoppers using the food chain.
(d) A farmer says killing the snakes did the plot good, since there are now fewer grasshoppers. Weigh his view against what happened to the eagles, and give a reasoned judgement.
questions.a: (a) Grass is the producer; the snake is at the fourth trophic level. (b) Frogs: (105 - 60) / 60 x 100 = 75% rise; grasshoppers: (400 - 250) / 400 x 100 = 37.5% fall. (c) With few snakes left to eat them, more frogs survived; more frogs ate more grasshoppers, so the grasshoppers fell. (d) He is partly right: fewer grasshoppers may mean less grass eaten. But the eagles lost their food (the snakes) and were no longer seen, and the frogs rose unchecked; one change spread along the whole chain and disturbed the plot's balance. Overall, killing the snakes did more harm than good to the ecosystem.
s: (a) Grass; fourth trophic level
(b) 75% rise in frogs and 37.5% fall in grasshoppers
(c) Fewer snakes, so more frogs, which ate more grasshoppers
(d) Judgement that weighs fewer grasshoppers against the loss of eagles and the disturbed balance

questions.q:
In a mango orchard live mango trees, hares that eat the grass and fallen leaves beneath them, foxes that hunt the hares and also eat fallen fruit, and fungi and bacteria growing on rotting leaves.
(a) Name the producer and say how it gets its food.
(b) Name the consumers and classify each as a herbivore, carnivore or omnivore.
(c) Name the decomposers and say what they do.
(d) Explain how these three groups together keep the soil of the orchard fertile.
questions.a: (a) The mango tree is the producer (autotroph); it makes its own food by photosynthesis. (b) The hare is a herbivore; the fox is an omnivore, since it eats both hares and fruit. (c) The fungi and bacteria are decomposers (saprotrophs); they break down the complex substances in dead leaves and other dead matter into simpler ones. (d) Producers make food that passes to the consumers; dead leaves, fruit and animal waste are broken down by the decomposers, which return nutrients to the soil; the trees take up these nutrients again, so nothing is wasted and the soil stays fertile.
s: (a) Mango tree, making food by photosynthesis
(b) Hare: herbivore; fox: omnivore
(c) Fungi and bacteria break down dead matter into simpler substances
(d) The cycle: producers feed consumers, decomposers return nutrients to the soil for the trees

questions.q: In which kind of relationship does one organism benefit while the other is harmed?
questions.a: Parasitism

questions.q: An orchid grows on the branch of a tree, and the tree branch is not affected. What does the orchid get from the tree?
questions.a: Physical support
o: Food made in the tree's leaves
Water drawn from the tree's roots

questions.q: After large numbers of frog legs were exported in the 1980s, the Government of India banned the export. Which of these was NOT an expected result of protecting the frogs?
questions.a: Frog populations would keep falling
o: Fewer insect pests in farm fields
Less harm to soil and water quality

questions.q:
Read these statements.
I. The balance of an ecosystem is fixed and does not change.
II. Competition for food, water, physical space or sunlight helps control the size of populations.
III. In parasitism, both organisms are harmed.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II only

questions.q:
The chapter says the balance of an ecosystem is 'dynamic, not fixed'.
(a) What does this mean?
(b) Name the two kinds of change that can disrupt this balance.
questions.a: (a) An ecosystem is in balance when the interactions among organisms and their environment keep populations and resources stable; this balance keeps adjusting and does not stay frozen at exact numbers. (b) Natural changes and human-made changes.
s: (a) Balance means interactions keep populations and resources stable, but it keeps adjusting rather than being fixed
(b) Natural and human-made changes

questions.q:
Two kinds of grass grow together in a park lawn.
(a) Name two resources the two grasses may compete for.
(b) According to the chapter, what could happen if one kind of grass faced no competition at all?
questions.a: (a) Any two of water, physical space and sunlight. (b) Competition helps control population size; without it, that grass could multiply too much and spread over the lawn, causing an imbalance in the ecosystem.
s: (a) Two of water, physical space and sunlight
(b) It could multiply too much and cause an imbalance

questions.q:
Name the relationship shown by each pair, and say which partner benefits.
(a) A leech sucks blood from a buffalo's leg, which becomes sore.
(b) A butterfly sips nectar from a flower and carries its pollen to another flower.
(c) A sparrow builds its nest in the branches of a neem tree, which is not affected.
questions.a: (a) Parasitism: the leech benefits and the buffalo is harmed. (b) Mutualism: both benefit, since the butterfly gets nectar and the flower gets pollinated. (c) Commensalism: the sparrow benefits and the tree is not affected.
s: (a) Parasitism, leech benefits
(b) Mutualism, both benefit
(c) Commensalism, sparrow benefits

questions.q:
Farmers in one district kept records of the frogs on their field bunds and the pesticide they used (illustrative figures). In 1978 they counted an average of 40 frogs per 100 m of bund and used 2 kg of synthetic pesticide per hectare. By 1985, when frogs were being caught on a large scale for the export of frog legs, they counted 12 frogs per 100 m and used 5 kg per hectare. Ten years after the export ban, they counted 30 frogs per 100 m and used 3 kg per hectare.
(a) What do frogs eat, and which feeding group does that put them in?
(b) By what percentage did the frogs fall from 1978 to 1985, and how many times as much pesticide was used in 1985 as in 1978?
(c) Explain the link between the fall in frogs and the rise in pesticide use.
(d) Do the figures support the view that the ban helped? Use the chapter's idea of a dynamic balance to explain why the numbers did not return exactly to the 1978 level.
questions.a: (a) Frogs eat insects, so they are carnivores (small carnivores, at the third trophic level in a chain such as grass -> grasshopper -> frog). (b) Fall = (40 - 12) / 40 x 100 = 70%; pesticide = 5 / 2 = 2.5 times as much. (c) Large-scale harvesting cut the frog population; with fewer frogs eating insects, agricultural pests rose, which forced farmers to use more synthetic pesticides. (d) Yes, largely: after the ban the frogs recovered to 30 (75% of the 1978 count) and pesticide use fell to 3 kg. The balance of an ecosystem is dynamic, not fixed, so populations settle at levels that keep adjusting rather than returning to exactly the earlier numbers.
s: (a) Insects; carnivores (small carnivores)
(b) 70% fall and 2.5 times the pesticide
(c) Fewer frogs, more pests, more pesticide
(d) Figures support the ban (frogs up to 30, pesticide down to 3 kg) and dynamic balance explains why not back to 1978 levels

questions.q:
A farmer in Karnataka keeps honeybee boxes at the edge of one half of his sunflower field (illustrative figures). The half with the bee boxes gave 1,800 kg of seed and the half without them gave 1,200 kg.
(a) Name the relationship between the honeybees and the sunflowers, and say what each partner gets.
(b) Find the percentage increase in seed in the half with the bee boxes.
(c) Explain, using pollination, why that half gave more seed.
(d) If dragonflies became very common around his field, how could his seed yield change? Use the chapter's pond study.
questions.a: (a) Mutualism: the bees get nectar and the flowers get pollinated. (b) (1800 - 1200) / 1200 x 100 = 50% more. (c) Bees carry pollen from the stamens to the carpels of the flowers; pollination is essential for the formation of seeds, so more bee visits meant more flowers pollinated and more seed. (d) Dragonflies eat bees, flies and butterflies, so more dragonflies would mean fewer bees, less pollination and a lower seed yield.
s: (a) Mutualism: bees get nectar, flowers get pollinated
(b) 50% increase
(c) More bees carry more pollen to carpels, so more flowers form seeds
(d) Dragonflies eat bees, so fewer pollinators and a lower yield

questions.a: (a) With fewer plants, less oxygen is produced in the water. (b) Less oxygen leads to a drop in the fish population. (c) With fewer fish, there are fewer consumers in the pond to eat the insects, so the insects increase in number. (d) The insects spread to nearby farmland and damage crops, so farmers are compelled to use pesticides, which may again harm the environment. (e) One small change (plants dying) sets off a chain of further changes, each causing the next, and the effects spread step by step from the pond to the farms.
s: (a) Fewer plants, less oxygen in the water
(b) Less oxygen, so the fish population drops
(c) Fewer fish (consumers), so insects increase
(d) Insects spread to farms; farmers use pesticides that harm the environment
(e) One change leads to a chain of other changes, spreading step by step

questions.q: What are protected areas? Name any two types of protected area found in India.
questions.a: Protected areas are parts of land or water set aside to conserve wildlife and their habitats. Types: any two of national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves and community conserved areas.

Two correct types, such as national parks and wildlife sanctuaries

questions.q: True or False? 'UNESCO declared the Sundarbans a World Heritage Site in 1987 because they faced no threat from human activity.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. UNESCO declared the Sundarbans a World Heritage Site in 1987 because of their importance: the largest mangrove forests in the world, home to many endangered species, and a shield against storm winds and waves. They are in fact under serious threat from mangroves being cut for fuelwood and farming, illegal hunting, overuse of forest resources and pollution.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: declared for its importance, and it is under serious threat from human activities such as cutting mangroves, hunting and pollution

questions.q:
The chapter names threats to the Sundarbans. For each threat below, say whether it damages the living (biotic) part or the non-living (abiotic) part of the ecosystem first, and how.
(a) Mangrove trees cut for fuelwood and farming
(b) Illegal hunting and overuse of forest resources
(c) Industrial waste and untreated sewage in the rivers
questions.a: (a) Biotic: the mangrove trees themselves are removed, so the forest that slows strong winds and waves and is home to many species shrinks. (b) Biotic: the wildlife living there is reduced, and many of these species are already endangered. (c) Abiotic: the river water is polluted, which damages the habitat of the organisms living in it.
s: (a) Biotic: loss of the mangrove trees and what they do
(b) Biotic: loss of wildlife, many species endangered
(c) Abiotic: polluted water damages the habitat

questions.q:
A city in Madhya Pradesh turned an old garbage dump into a park with trees, a small pond and walking paths (illustrative figures). Before the park, students counted 5 kinds of birds at the site; five years later they counted 20 kinds. A dust monitor at the site read 150 units before the park and 105 units after it. Gardeners water, prune and clean the park every week.
(a) Is the park a natural or a human-made ecosystem? Give one way it differs from a natural forest.
(b) Find the percentage rise in the kinds of birds and the percentage fall in the dust reading.
(c) Which benefits of well-designed human-made ecosystems, named in the chapter, do these figures show?
(d) Next year the city can fund only one project: a second park like this, or protecting an old natural wetland outside the city. Give one argument for each, and make a reasoned choice.
questions.a: (a) A human-made ecosystem; unlike a natural forest, it needs human care and management (the weekly watering, pruning and cleaning). (b) Birds: (20 - 5) / 5 x 100 = 300% rise; dust: (150 - 105) / 150 x 100 = 30% fall. (c) Reducing pollution (less dust) and supporting biodiversity (more kinds of birds); it also gives people recreational space. (d) For a second park: it would cut pollution and give recreation where people live. For the wetland: a natural ecosystem supports many organisms without constant human care, and protecting existing habitats saves nature for the future, while a lost wetland cannot easily be rebuilt. A reasoned choice of either, using these points, earns the mark (for example, protect the wetland first because it already exists and needs no upkeep).
s: (a) Human-made; needs human care and management
(b) 300% rise in kinds of birds and 30% fall in dust
(c) Reduces pollution and supports biodiversity (and recreation)
(d) One argument for each option and a reasoned choice

questions.a: (a) A food crisis, caused by low crop production. (b) Tractors, machines, synthetic fertilisers and pesticides. (c) Food production rose, which helped India become food secure. (d) Any three: overuse of synthetic chemicals; excessive groundwater extraction; growing only one crop (monoculture) for commercial gain, which reduces biodiversity and affects pollinators; overuse of fertilisers lowers humus and friendly soil microorganisms, leaving soil prone to erosion; fewer natural predators, so more pests; pests developing resistance to pesticides. (e) Organic and natural farming that reduce synthetic fertilisers, and nourishing the soil with organic manure such as Kunapa Jala and compost, as Vrikshayurveda advises. Judgement: the statement is fair, because the methods met the food need, but their overuse harms soil, water and biodiversity.
s: (a) Food crisis due to low crop production
(b) Tractors, machines, synthetic fertilisers and pesticides
(c) Raised food production, making India food secure
(d) Three correct reasons the methods are unsustainable
(e) Two sustainable practices and a reasoned judgement

questions.q:
A coastal village has a 50-hectare belt of mangrove forest between some of its houses and the sea (illustrative figures). In a storm in 2020, 6% of the houses behind the mangrove belt were damaged, while 42% of the houses on an open stretch of shore without mangroves were damaged. Some villagers now want to clear 20 hectares of the belt for paddy fields.
(a) Name two ways mangrove forests help people and the air, as the chapter describes.
(b) How many times as large was the share of damaged houses on the open shore as behind the mangroves?
(c) What percentage of the mangrove belt would be cleared?
(d) The chapter names cutting mangroves for farming as a threat. Explain why, using the storm figures.
(e) Suggest a decision for the village that weighs the need for farmland against safety, and justify it.
questions.a: (a) Mangroves slow down strong winds and waves during storms and floods, and their trees absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen. (b) 42 / 6 = 7 times as large. (c) 20 / 50 x 100 = 40% of the belt. (d) Damage was 7 times higher where there were no mangroves, so cutting the belt would remove the protection that slows the winds and waves and put the houses behind it at much greater risk; it would also destroy the home of many organisms. (e) For example: keep the mangrove belt and find farmland elsewhere, since the safety of the houses and the ecosystem outweighs the extra paddy; any decision that weighs both needs and is justified with the figures earns the mark.
s: (a) Slows storm winds and waves; absorbs carbon dioxide and releases oxygen
(b) 7 times
(d) Uses the 7-times figure to explain the loss of protection
(e) A justified decision weighing farmland against safety
